title: New Partnerships for Action. Building on the Capital of Environmental Psychology and Architecture
research_question: How can engaging architecture students in live design projects with community groups, in collaboration with environmental psychology students, develop student skills, positively impact communities, and improve society's perception of academic institutions, particularly in the context of urban regeneration?

participants.description: Architecture students (University of Strathclyde, UK), Environmental Psychology Master's students (University of Surrey, UK), and community groups (Sighthill and Govanhill communities in Glasgow, UK), including resident associations, youth, language, elderly, sport, and mothers' groups.
participants.recruitment: Community Design Unit invited by local Tenants Association (Sighthill) and Govanhill community.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Live design projects in two inner-city Glasgow neighborhoods: Sighthill (deprived, disconnected, high immigrant population, poor housing, insufficient social facilities, racial intolerance) and Govanhill (residential, diverse population, sub-standard housing, derelict sites, high unemployment).

mechanisms: Involving community groups in the design process creates responsive environments by incorporating their needs and desires, leading to higher satisfaction.

Engaging architecture students in live projects with community groups, supported by environmental psychology, provides a realistic learning experience that develops intellectual, critical, professional, and social skills.

Collaboration between different disciplines (architecture and environmental psychology) enriches the learning process by providing diverse perspectives and methods for understanding human-environment relationships.

The Multi Modal Strategy (MMS) provides a structured approach to gather community input, ensuring design solutions are based on a comprehensive understanding of an area's qualities and deficiencies, rather than solely on designers' assumptions.
Action learning and participatory design approaches foster a heightened sense of responsibility and realism in students, leading to more relevant and sustainable design outcomes.
Community groups gain evaluative and critical skills, confidence in discussion, and in-depth knowledge of their area through exposure to design processes and technical expertise.
implementation_implications: Design professionals should cooperate with experts from other fields (e.g., environmental psychology) to reinforce design solutions and create responsive environments.
Architectural education should integrate live design projects with community groups to develop students' intellectual, critical, professional, and social skills.
Curriculum development should focus on bringing architectural education and environmental psychology together, potentially through joint Master courses.

Community capacity building should be supported by involving residents in design processes, providing them with informal training on environmental issues, and fostering their evaluative and critical skills.
Design interventions in deprived urban areas should be precisely targeted to maximize scarce resources and ensure people's interaction with physical space induces sustainable performance.

Academic institutions should clearly define project goals and manage expectations for both students and community groups, acknowledging that student projects may primarily yield ideas rather than immediate concrete outcomes.
Establishing clear roles, competencies, and commitment levels within interdisciplinary design teams is crucial for successful collaboration.
Incorporating social rituals (e.g., communal meals) into meetings can facilitate informal communication and information exchange between students and community members.
Traditional studio culture in architecture education needs to evolve to encourage specialization and critical thinking, moving beyond stylistic and personal approaches.

tables.description: Positive sides of teaching collaborative projects and social design in schools, categorized by repercussions on Education/students, Community groups, and Environment.
Risks that the collaborative/participative process can generate, categorized by repercussions on Education/students and Community groups.
Limitations and practical issues to take into account, categorized by repercussions on Education/students, Community groups, and Environment.

limitations: The interpretation of clients' needs/wants is complex and requires preparation to prevent gross assumptions.
Designers need a good degree of precision in searching for and making use of information to build a design scenario and make informed choices.
Student projects very rarely can deliver concrete and finite outcomes.

Academic priorities must be clear; clients must be aware that what they can obtain from this experience is - for the moment - simply a repertoire of ideas. Further developments are expected to be produced, but this will require time and experience.
It is important to define roles, competencies and levels of commitment within the team.
An initial central core in community organization helps save time but risks being less open to students' contribution.
Users' requirements and goals often won't coincide with academic requirements and goals.
When working with large communities, it cannot be assumed that those willing to be directly involved will accept to overcome social, racial, cultural, political barriers and get along well together.
Students often find it hard to adjust to the new condition of interdisciplinary collaboration, tending to be defensive and patronizing due to traditional studio culture.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural or restorative environments and engaging in meaningful activities can replenish directed attention capacity and foster well-being.
The principles of restorative environments can be applied to collaborative design projects and community partnerships to enhance student engagement, learning, and personal growth.
